items.title: John Levy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Calloway and became a great, great player in the studios

ctx.x: It’s kind of hard for – your question. But anyway, music, it was just a means to an end. It was a means to make an extra amount of money to take care of a family once you got married. It was just a means. I wasn’t – there’s no special plan or no special idea about it. It was just – I could play a bass. I picked it up. I could play it. Then I had certain musicians help me, who were well schooled, like Milton Hinton and Truck Parham, who at that time – Milt ended up with Cab

Calloway and became a great, great player in the studios – great musician. They helped me. They taught me. In those days, musicians would help each other. If you heard something, they’d show you how to play it and how it worked, the fingering and all that sort of thing. I had books. I studied the books and practiced at home, but I didn’t really go in to have formal lessons. I was able to read, because having those lessons from the violin taught me time and all that, as far as notes were concerned. It was just in…
Can you talk about the Depression, in particular your mother’s death?

items.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: before he joined Cab he was working for $35 a week

ctx.x: Yeah, they probably remember better than I do what it was. But it wasn’t much I’ll tell you that.
I remember Milt I think was saying that before he joined Cab he was working for $35 a week, and you know then he went with Cab and it tripled and he said, “I’m a millionaire.”

Well I know I worked, I worked in night clubs in Chicago coming along and made $50 a week, and that was, that was big money, you know? It wasn’t big money, it was just enough to get by on, but my first experience of really making money was really with George Shearing because up to that point, even with Buddy Rich and with the Stuff Smith things was pretty good, but the real money, the real money came with — for me — came with George Shearing, and then of course the experience and all that. But I was fortunate,…
